IO3_transformations.algorithm: Check user_id not already reacted with same emoji. Insert into reactions table. Increment count.
Delete reaction from table. Decrement count.
Group reactions by emoji. Count per emoji. Check current user's reactions.

P.P1_bottleneck_analysis: Real-time sync of reaction counts across multiple users (WebSocket or polling). Duplicate reaction prevention (database constraint). Reaction notification delivery (should not spam author).
P.P2_defensibility: Fixed emoji set (OK, !, ?, +1, thumbs-down) prevents misuse and is culturally neutral. Database unique constraint prevents duplicates. Real-time sync is expected for modern UX. Notifications optional (can mute).
P.P3_confidence_level: Very high confidence. Simple CRUD operations. Real-time sync is well-established pattern.
P4_failure_modes: Duplicate reaction creation → count is wrong (mitigate: unique constraint on (message_id, user_id, emoji))
Reaction count out of sync across devices → user confusion (mitigate: periodic recount on reconnection)
Reaction notification spam → user disables all notifications (mitigate: rate limit (max 1 notification per minute per message))
P.P5_backup_plan: If reaction fails: show error, user can retry. If sync fails: user sees stale count until refresh. If notification fails: user still sees reaction count updated.
P.P6_backup_plan_test: Simulate database constraint violation (try duplicate reaction). Simulate sync failure (disconnect network). Simulate notification failure (mock FCM). Test edge case: remove own reaction while notification sending.
P.P7_testing_strategy: Unit tests for reaction CRUD. Integration tests for sync across multiple users. Load tests for high-traffic messages (100+ reactions per second). End-to-end tests for full user flow (add, remove, see count update). Stress test: 10k users all reacting to same message simultaneously.
P.P8_benchmarks: Add/remove reaction: <200ms. Sync to other users: <500ms (WebSocket) or <2s (polling). Count accuracy: 100%. No duplicates (database enforced). Notification delivery: >95% within 10s.

L.L1_legal_considerations: Reactions can enable harassment (e.g., multiple users reacting negatively to isolate a user). Mitigate with moderation tools (admin can remove reactions). Emoji misinterpretation across cultures (mitigate: use simple, unambiguous emoji only).
L.L3_consent_requirements: Users implicitly consent to reactions by participating in messages. No separate consent.
L.L4_liability_notes: Harassment via reactions is possible. Mitigation: moderation tools, ability to mute threads, reporting workflow. Clear community guidelines on reaction misuse.

F.F1_cost_considerations: Reactions table storage: ~100B per reaction. Negligible compute cost.
F.F3_revenue_impact: Reactions increase engagement and stickiness. Minor positive impact.

S.S1_cybersecurity: No sensitive data in reactions. Rate limiting on reaction send (prevent abuse: max 10 reactions per user per message per hour). User cannot remove others' reactions.
S.S2_data_privacy: Reaction data is public within thread. User identity revealed (who reacted). Archive/delete message cascade-deletes reactions.
S.S3_encryption_requirements: Reactions stored plaintext (not encrypted). Metadata only, no content risk.
S.S4_access_control: Only user can remove their own reaction. Thread members can see all reactions. Admin can moderate (remove reactions if harassment).
S.S5_audit_requirements: Audit log of reaction additions/removals (for moderation investigation). Audit trail retention: 1 year.

X.X1_notes: Reactions are lightweight engagement feature. Fixed emoji set is more secure than custom emoji (prevents malicious content). Real-time sync expectations are high for modern apps. Moderation tools important for preventing harassment.
X2_open_questions: Fixed emoji set or custom? (fixed is simpler and safer)
Which emoji to include? (OK, !, ?, +1, thumbs-down, or expand?)
Notification for every reaction or rate-limited? (rate limit probably needed)
Can admins remove reactions? (for moderation, yes)
X.X3_related_research: Slack reactions. Discord reactions. Harassment and engagement patterns in social platforms. Emoji accessibility guidelines.
